rationale: The target is the ary3 Shootout kernel: a ~512-byte binary dominated by a single tight, data-parallel matrix-multiply loop in main, so virtually all execution time sits in one hot basic block and any control-flow-heavy transformation is paid on every iteration. I therefore keep the two cheap, semantically local passes favored — SUB (instruction substitution) and SPLIT (basic-block splitting) — with high weights across all dimensions since their runtime and size costs are near zero and their correctness risk is negligible, giving solid diversity for a tiny function count (only main matters). IGV and IBR get moderate security/diversity weights but suppressed cost weights: IGV complicates CFG recovery meaningfully but adds global-variable traffic in the hot loop, and IBR's opaque predicates execute per-iteration, so both should apply only where features indicate cold paths. ICALL is kept low across the board because indirect-call conversion of arithmetic-heavy code defeats loop optimization and its static analysis value on a 474-byte main is limited. BCF and FLA are retained in the table only with minimal weights and heavily suppressed cost dimensions — full flattening or bogus-control-flow duplication of the kernel would inflate runtime and text size by multiples on a loop-dominated benchmark, far exceeding an acceptable overhead budget, while correctness risk from loop-carried restructurings is nonzero. Net effect: baseline obscuring substitutions everywhere, structural noise on cold regions, and the hot kernel left optimizable.
